geographic_scope: Statewide; over or near defined critical infrastructure and critical systems
source_title: Protection of critical infrastructure and systems from drones
uas_topic: Critical infrastructure; intentional photography; loitering; crime facilitation; explosive payloads
regulated_party: Any person operating or using a UAS or model aircraft, subject to statutory exceptions
regulated_activity: Operating over or near critical infrastructure or a critical system to intentionally photograph it, intentionally loiter, further another crime, or carry an explosive device
requirement_type: Criminal prohibition with statutory exceptions and counter-UAS enforcement authority
permit_or_approval_required: No state permit stated; an exception applies to an FAA-authorized person whose operation complies with that authorization or FAA rules, and other listed exceptions may apply
summary: W.S. 19-13-503 prohibits specified intentional UAS conduct over or near a broadly defined list of critical infrastructure and critical systems, including energy, water, communications, rail, public-safety, correctional, military, hospital, mining, and manufacturing facilities. It lists exceptions for FAA-authorized compliant operations, government-owned UAS, owners or their agents, specified emergency users, and private landowners on their own property. A first offense is a misdemeanor and a later offense a felony; law enforcement may disable, damage, or remove a violating aircraft.
verification_status: Verified directly against current Title 19 and the official 2025 bill summary/digest
notes: The statute does not define “near” or prescribe documentation for the FAA-authorization exception. Chapter 112 was enacted after the Legislature overrode the governor's veto.

source_title: Unmanned aircraft systems and correctional institutions
uas_topic: Correctional facilities; surveillance; recording; contraband; weapons
regulated_party: Any person using a covered UAS, subject to enumerated exclusions
regulated_activity: Intentional UAS trespass over or in a correctional facility or its grounds to photograph, surveil, broadcast, record, convey contraband, or deliver a deadly weapon
requirement_type: Criminal prohibition; facility authorization exception; notice for specified excluded governmental uses
permit_or_approval_required: Yes — authorization by the person in charge of the institution or facility
summary: Except as authorized by the person in charge, W.S. 6-5-214 prohibits intentional UAS trespass over or in a penal institution, correctional facility, or its grounds for recording or surveillance, conveying contraband, or delivering a deadly weapon. Recording and contraband offenses are misdemeanors punishable by up to one year and $2,000; a deadly-weapon delivery offense is a felony punishable by up to ten years and $10,000. Specified federal, state, law-enforcement, and emergency uses are excluded, with reasonable-notice requirements for listed excluded uses.
verification_status: Verified directly against current Title 6 and 2023 Enrolled Act 67
notes: The facility's person in charge is the statutory approving authority. The statute authorizes reasonable defensive actions consistent with Department of Corrections rules.

source_title: Use of aircraft for hunting or taking wildlife prohibited; UAV included
regulated_party: Any person using an aircraft, expressly including an unmanned aerial vehicle
regulated_activity: Harassing, pursuing, hunting, shooting, or killing specified wildlife with or from aircraft; using aircraft to aid in taking wildlife
requirement_type: Criminal prohibition with governmental-duty and limited hunter exceptions
permit_or_approval_required: No general permit stated; statute exempts governmental agencies, employees, contractors, or designees performing lawful duties
aec_relevance: High for wildlife and environmental missions
summary: W.S. 23-3-306 prohibits using aircraft to harass, pursue, hunt, shoot, or kill wildlife that requires a license or permit, is protected, or is federally threatened or endangered. It also prohibits using aircraft to aid the taking of wildlife—other than predatory animals—by spotting, locating, communicating, or otherwise assisting. For this section, “aircraft” expressly includes an unmanned aerial vehicle. Government agencies and their employees, contractors, or designees performing lawful duties are exempt; violations are classified as high misdemeanors.
notes: The statute's governmental-duty exception is source- and mission-specific; it does not create a general commercial-purpose exception.

source_title: General Hunting Regulation — aircraft spotting and UAV definition
regulated_party: Persons using aircraft, including UAVs, in connection with taking game
regulated_activity: Using an aircraft with intent to spot, locate, and aid in taking big game or trophy game during specified periods
commercial_operator_relevance: Low for ordinary commercial work; high if imagery supports hunting
summary: Current Chapter 2 defines “aircraft” to include an unmanned aerial vehicle. Section 12 prohibits using aircraft with intent to spot, locate, and aid in taking any big-game animal from August 1 through January 31 of the following year. It also prohibits using aircraft to spot, locate, and aid in taking any trophy-game animal during an open season. The rule excludes ordinary aircraft operation when there is no attempt or intent to locate game. The Commission adopted the 2026 Chapter 2 regulation as proposed.
verification_status: Verified against current official 2026 regulation materials and Commission adoption notice
notes: Chapter 2 is updated annually; recheck the current year's regulation before wildlife-season fieldwork.

regulated_activity: Large-UAS takeoff, landing, operation, accidents, and injuries

permit_or_approval_required: No state permit identified in this pass; current Commission rules should be checked for a non-small-UAS mission

summary: Title 10 directs the Aeronautics Commission to adopt reasonable rules governing where statutory “unmanned aircraft” may take off and land, permits certain operating rules subject to federal limits, and requires immediate reporting to the Commission of aircraft accidents or injuries in Wyoming. The same title defines “unmanned aircraft” by reference to 14 C.F.R. 1.1 but expressly excludes “small unmanned aircraft” as federally defined. These provisions therefore do not establish a Wyoming accident-reporting or takeoff/landing rule for a typical under-55-pound small UAS.

notes: No current Aeronautics Commission rule applying these provisions to non-small UAS was located by keyword in the state rules system.

source_title: Low or dangerous flight; landing on land or water of another
effective_date: Effective immediately in 2017; amended in 2018; current codification
uas_topic: Large-UAS low flight; dangerous flight; landowner consent for landing
regulated_party: Operators of statutory “unmanned aircraft,” which expressly excludes federally defined small unmanned aircraft
regulated_activity: Low or imminently dangerous flight and landing on another person's land or water
requirement_type: Criminal prohibition and civil damage rule
permit_or_approval_required: Landowner consent is required for a non-forced landing by a covered aircraft
commercial_operator_relevance: Low for typical Part 107 fleets; high for aircraft outside the small-UAS definition
summary: W.S. 10-4-303 states that flight by covered aircraft is lawful unless it is low enough to interfere with the owner's existing land or water use, is imminently dangerous to persons or property, or violates federal air-commerce rules. Landing on another's land or water without consent is unlawful except for a forced landing, with liability for actual forced-landing damage. An unlawful unmanned-aircraft operation under subsection (a) is a misdemeanor. Title 10's definition expressly excludes federally defined small unmanned aircraft, limiting this provision's UAS application.
notes: The UAS-specific misdemeanor in subsection (d) carries up to six months' imprisonment, a fine up to $750, or both.

geographic_scope: Statewide legal context for small-UAS overflight
citation: LSO memorandum to Joint Judiciary Committee, May 13, 2022, pp. 5–6
revision_date: No later official UAS-specific judicial resolution located through 2026-08-02
uas_topic: Small-UAS aerial trespass; intrusion upon seclusion; privacy
regulated_activity: Low overflight that interferes with property use; intrusive observation of private affairs
requirement_type: Official legal research describing unresolved common-law exposure
summary: The official LSO memorandum describes small-UAS trespass law as unsettled. It states that Wyoming recognizes the common-law tort of intrusion upon seclusion and that the tort may apply to a UAS flying closely over private property when the intrusion into private affairs would be highly offensive to a reasonable person. It also explains that common-law aerial trespass may turn on entry into the immediate reaches of the airspace plus substantial interference with use and enjoyment, while noting that no Wyoming case on point was located and Title 10 excludes small UAS.
verification_status: Verified directly against the official LSO memorandum; no controlling Wyoming UAS decision located
notes: This is nonbinding research, not a statute, regulation, attorney-general opinion, or court holding. A 2025 bill proposing a 200-foot small-UAS trespass crime was not enacted.

citation: Wyoming Drone Hub operator notification webpage
regulated_party: Drone operators planning flights in Wyoming
regulated_activity: Submitting planned flight location and timing to the state Drone Hub
permit_or_approval_required: No — the webpage requests notification but does not state that it is a permit or mandatory filing
summary: The Wyoming Department of Homeland Security's Drone Hub asks operators to provide planned flight information so reported sightings can be compared with known lawful activity. Its operator page links a pre-flight notification form and frames the request as “Please let us know when/where you'll be flying,” not as a license, permit, or mandatory state filing. The page therefore documents a voluntary coordination channel rather than an operator authorization requirement. It is distinct from any FAA authorization and does not replace property-owner or state-agency approval.
verification_status: Verified directly against the current official Drone Hub operator page
notes: The Drone Hub is operated by the Wyoming Department of Homeland Security.
